rationale: A wins because it knows the difference between a story and a claim that still needs proof. Its "Who is responsible for a flight when no one is flying it?" angle turns the no-pilot fact into a specific regulatory beat with the right missing evidence, while B leads with "no named utility willing to say so" and "pay a premium to avoid Chinese hardware," both of which add facts the update did not give. B has usable bones, but the headlines keep writing checks the release cannot cash.
gaps_in_A: "The trade desk will take a week-long operations piece" overclaims editorial appetite. That should be conditional on a named utility, deployment detail, and a defect example.
"bought and budgeted like a sensor installation" is a smart test, but still a test. The update gives docked autonomy, not procurement model or budget treatment.
"regulators have been slow to accommodate" imports context the update did not supply. Plausible, but it needs current FAA/BVLOS evidence before becoming a premise.
"defense-and-security trade" is borderline beat drift unless the import-restriction angle is tied to a real security-policy hook. The product facts are utilities and infrastructure, not defense.
gaps_in_B: "no named utility willing to say so" invents motive. The update says no named utility is disclosed, not that utilities refused to attach their names.
"the grid will pay a premium to avoid Chinese hardware" invents both a price premium and buyer motive. The proof section asks for those facts because the headline does not have them.

"the launch is the first concrete evidence of where the 2024 exit led" invents "first." The update says Skydio exited consumer drones two years ago, not that nothing enterprise-relevant shipped or was covered since.
"without a human in the loop" overstates the facts. No pilot and automated defect reports do not prove no human review, remote supervision, or signoff.
